impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the six-year statute of limitations in 28 U.S.C. § 2501 for claims against the government in the Court of Federal Claims is subject to American Pipe tolling, and whether the Federal Circuit's prior decision in Bright v. United States was implicitly overruled by the Supreme Court's decision in California Public Employees' Retirement System v. ANZ Securities, Inc.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held that 28 U.S.C. § 2501 is not subject to American Pipe tolling, recognizing that part of its prior decision in Bright v. United States was implicitly overruled by the Supreme Court's ANZ Securities decision. This ruling forecloses class action tolling for government takings and breach of contract claims brought in the Court of Federal Claims.
impacts.negativeImplications: Businesses and investors who relied on class action filings to toll the statute of limitations for government takings or breach of contract claims at the Court of Federal Claims will lose the ability to file individual claims after the class action ends if the six-year limitations period has expired, significantly narrowing the window for recovery.

impacts.caseName: Teva Pharmaceuticals International GmbH v. Eli Lilly and Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Circuit's enablement analysis for broad method-of-treatment claims comports with Supreme Court enablement precedent, and whether overly broad genus claims covering humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies for treating headache satisfy the enablement requirement.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit denied en banc rehearing of a panel decision upholding Teva's broad method-of-treatment patent claims covering anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies for treating headache. Judge Dyk dissented, arguing the panel's holding creates confusion about enablement standards for method claims and will sustain overly broad claims that undermine medical innovation. The case has significant implications for pharmaceutical patent scope after the Supreme Court's Amgen decision.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders with broad method-of-treatment claims benefit from the panel's more permissive enablement standard, which may allow broader genus claims to survive validity challenges, particularly in the biologics space.
impacts.negativeImplications: Competitors, biosimilar manufacturers, and generic drug companies face a broader blocking patent landscape, as the decision may sustain overly broad method claims that restrict competition and innovation in the pharmaceutical and biologics industries.

impacts.caseName: Dental Monitoring SAS v. Align Technology, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the PTAB's Penumbra framework—which diverges from the Federal Circuit's Dynamic Drinkware precedent—correctly determines the prior art effective date of a reference patent under AIA 35 U.S.C. § 102(d)(2) by requiring only that the provisional application describe the subject matter relied upon, rather than requiring written description support for at least one claim of the non-provisional patent.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the PTAB's obviousness determination and remanded, addressing the critical question of how to determine a reference patent's prior art effective date under the AIA. The Board had applied its Penumbra framework rather than Dynamic Drinkware to conclude a reference patent qualified as prior art based on its provisional filing date. This decision has significant implications for IPR proceedings and patent validity determinations.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners benefit from potential limitations on how early a prior art date can be assigned to reference patents in IPR proceedings, potentially preserving the validity of patents that would otherwise be invalidated by earlier-dated prior art.
impacts.negativeImplications: IPR petitioners and companies seeking to challenge patents may face greater difficulty establishing prior art dates for reference patents, potentially making it harder to invalidate competitor patents through IPR proceedings.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the trial court was required to defer to the terms of a license agreement in assessing copyright infringement damages, and whether the trial court's use of the 'book of wisdom' and assessment of non-compensatory damages against the government were legally permissible.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the trial court's decision to assess copyright infringement damages via a hypothetical negotiation rather than deferring to license agreement terms, but vacated in part because the trial court adopted a legally impermissible view of the 'book of wisdom' and assessed non-compensatory damages against the government. This ruling provides important guidance on copyright damages methodology in government software infringement cases.
impacts.positiveImplications: Software companies and copyright holders benefit from the court's affirmation that hypothetical negotiation is a valid damages methodology even when a license agreement exists, potentially allowing for higher damages awards.
impacts.negativeImplications: The ruling constrains copyright holders by prohibiting non-compensatory damages against the government and limiting misuse of the 'book of wisdom' doctrine, which could reduce recoveries in government infringement cases.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether an exclusive licensee's shift from active product development to patent enforcement constitutes cessation of business operations triggering automatic termination of the license agreement, and whether the license conveyed 'all substantial rights' sufficient to allow the licensee to sue without joining the patent owner.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal, holding that TexasLDPC's exclusive license from Texas A&M did not automatically terminate when the company shifted its business to patent enforcement. The court also held that the license conveyed 'all substantial rights' in the patents, entitling the licensee to sue in its own name without joining the university. This decision clarifies the rights of exclusive licensees, including patent assertion entities, to enforce licensed patents.
impacts.positiveImplications: Exclusive licensees and patent assertion entities benefit from clarity that shifting to enforcement-focused business operations does not terminate license agreements, and that broadly drafted exclusive licenses can confer standing to sue without joining the patent owner.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers face a more difficult path to dismissal in suits brought by exclusive licensees, as challenges to standing based on license termination or failure to join the patent owner are less likely to succeed under this holding.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to non-uniform constellations for communication systems are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court correctly denied judgment as a matter of law on non-infringement and damages.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the district court's summary judgment of patent eligibility for certain claims while affirming eligibility for others, affirmed the denial of JMOL on non-infringement and damages, and remanded. The decision provides important guidance on the application of the Alice/Mayo framework to communication technology patents, distinguishing between claims that recite specific technical implementations and those that may be directed to abstract ideas.
impacts.positiveImplications: Technology companies benefit from the court's affirmation that some communication technology patent claims involving specific technical implementations satisfy § 101, supporting enforcement of patents covering standardized technologies.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face continued uncertainty under § 101, as the court vacated eligibility for certain claims, demonstrating that even within the same patent family, some claims may survive while others fail the Alice/Mayo test.

impacts.caseName: T-Mobile US, Inc. v. KAIFI LLC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Circuit has subject-matter jurisdiction over a dispute concerning interpretation of a patent settlement agreement's phrase 'survives the EPR,' or whether the case must be transferred to a regional circuit as a state law contract dispute.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held it lacked jurisdiction over a contract interpretation dispute arising from a patent litigation settlement agreement and transferred the case to the Fifth Circuit. The dispute centered on whether T-Mobile owed an additional payment to KAIFI after the PTO confirmed multiple asserted claims patentable without amendment in an ex parte reexamination. The court concluded that interpreting the settlement phrase 'survives the EPR' is a state law contract question, not a patent law question.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies drafting patent settlement agreements benefit from clarity that disputes over contract interpretation in settlement agreements will be resolved by regional circuits applying state contract law, which may provide more predictable outcomes.
impacts.negativeImplications: Parties to patent settlement agreements may face forum uncertainty, as disputes they expect to be heard by the Federal Circuit may be transferred to regional circuits, requiring different legal expertise and potentially different interpretive frameworks.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether Commerce's regulation requiring domestic interested parties to indicate intent to participate in antidumping sunset reviews within 15 days of notice of initiation conflicts with the governing statute, which is silent on such a deadline.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the Court of International Trade, holding that Commerce's 15-day filing deadline for domestic interested parties to indicate participation in antidumping duty sunset reviews is a permissible exercise of the agency's authority. The Trade Court had declared the regulation void, but the Federal Circuit found the statute silent on the timing question and the regulation the product of reasoned decision-making within delegated power.
impacts.positiveImplications: Domestic manufacturers seeking to maintain antidumping duty orders benefit from a clear, predictable 15-day deadline for indicating participation in sunset reviews, and the decision preserves Commerce's procedural framework for administering trade remedies.
impacts.negativeImplications: Domestic interested parties who miss the strict 15-day filing deadline risk having antidumping duty orders revoked, as the court upheld Commerce's authority to impose this tight timeline even though the statute does not expressly require it.

impacts.caseName: VDPP, LLC v. Volkswagen Group of America, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court abused its discretion in dismissing a patent infringement complaint without leave to amend and in awarding attorney fees under 35 U.S.C. § 285 and sanctioning plaintiff's counsel under 28 U.S.C. § 1927.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's dismissal of a patent infringement case with prejudice, denial of leave to amend, and award of $207,543.60 in attorney fees to the defendant under § 285, along with sanctions against plaintiff's counsel. The court found the plaintiff had implicitly agreed not to amend its complaint and that the proposed amended complaint was futile. This decision reinforces the consequences of filing frivolous patent infringement suits.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants in patent infringement cases benefit from the court's willingness to award substantial attorney fees and impose sanctions on plaintiffs and their counsel who pursue meritless claims, deterring abusive patent litigation.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders and their counsel face heightened risk of fee-shifting and personal sanctions when pursuing infringement claims that lack merit, particularly when there are indicators of claim weakness such as related applications rejected under § 101.

impacts.caseName: Range of Motion Products, LLC v. Armaid Company Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Circuit's Egyptian Goddess framework for design patent infringement improperly focuses on differences rather than overall similarity, and whether design patent claim construction involving functionality questions should be resolved by the jury rather than the court.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit denied en banc rehearing on the standard for design patent infringement under Egyptian Goddess. Chief Judge Moore dissented, arguing the court's framework has improperly shifted focus to dissimilarity and allowed courts to resolve infringement at summary judgment without adequate prior art examination. The concurrence defended the existing standard as consistent with Supreme Court and circuit precedent. This decision preserves the current design patent infringement framework with significant implications for product design protection.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies accused of design patent infringement benefit from the preserved framework that allows courts to resolve infringement at summary judgment when designs are sufficiently distinct, reducing litigation costs.
impacts.negativeImplications: Design patent holders face continued challenges enforcing their rights, as the current framework's emphasis on differences may make it easier for courts to grant summary judgment of non-infringement without jury consideration.

impacts.caseName: Ridge Corp. v. Kirk NationaLease Co.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly granted preliminary injunctive relief in a patent infringement case involving an insulated overhead door patent.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's grant of a preliminary injunction barring the defendants from making, using, selling, or importing products alleged to infringe a patent on insulated overhead doors. The reversal provides guidance on the standards for preliminary injunctive relief in patent cases, affecting competitors in the commercial door and refrigeration industries.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the Federal Circuit's willingness to reverse preliminary injunctions, reducing the risk of being forced out of markets before full adjudication of patent validity and infringement.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders seeking to preserve market exclusivity through preliminary injunctions face a higher bar, as the Federal Circuit's reversal signals close scrutiny of the requirements for such relief.

impacts.caseName: AML IP, LLC v. Bath & Body Works Direct, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a district court, after concluding venue is improper and dismissing on that ground, may also reach and decide a Rule 12(b)(6) motion based on patent ineligibility under 35 U.S.C. § 101.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's dual dismissal on both improper venue and patent ineligibility grounds, rejecting the argument that the court lacked authority to address the merits after finding venue improper. The '979 patent related to e-commerce methods using a 'bridge computer.' This holding allows courts to efficiently resolve both procedural and substantive defenses simultaneously in patent cases.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants benefit from the ability to obtain simultaneous dismissals on both venue and merits grounds, providing broader preclusive effect and discouraging refiling in other jurisdictions.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face the risk that venue challenges will be coupled with substantive invalidity rulings, potentially preventing them from asserting their patents in any forum after a single adverse ruling.

impacts.caseName: Satius Holding, LLC v. Samsung Electronics Co., Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to a communications apparatus for transmitting signals 'over air' using a coupler with a transformer having a non-magnetic core are invalid for lack of enablement under 35 U.S.C. § 112(a), even if they are not indefinite.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed invalidity of the asserted patent claims, but on enablement grounds rather than the indefiniteness basis used by the district court. The court reversed the lower court's indefiniteness finding while affirming the final judgment of invalidity on alternative grounds raised by Samsung. This decision illustrates the Federal Circuit's willingness to reach alternative invalidity theories to affirm judgments.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the court's willingness to affirm invalidity on alternative grounds not relied upon by the district court, providing additional paths to invalidate asserted patents.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face risk that even if they prevail on one invalidity defense, courts may affirm invalidity on alternative grounds raised by accused infringers but not addressed below.

impacts.caseName: KG Dongbu Steel Co., Ltd. v. United States
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Court of International Trade correctly sustained Commerce's determination that debt-to-equity conversions by a foreign government conferred no countervailable benefit on a steel manufacturer.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the Court of International Trade and instructed it to reinstate Commerce's original determinations that debt-to-equity conversions conferred countervailable benefits. The case addresses how Commerce evaluates whether government equity infusions to foreign manufacturers are inconsistent with usual private investor practices, a critical methodology in countervailing duty cases affecting international trade in steel and other commodities.
impacts.positiveImplications: Domestic manufacturers benefit from the reinstatement of Commerce's original subsidy findings, which may result in higher countervailing duties on competing imports and a more level playing field in the domestic market.
impacts.negativeImplications: Foreign exporters and U.S. importers face higher countervailing duties, and the decision may embolden Commerce to take more aggressive positions on evaluating government equity infusions as countervailable subsidies.
